newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan flirts with tax money for bad loans debate.
newsitem.headline: Japan flirts with tax money for bad loans debate.

text.p: Maverick Japanese politician Naoto Kan has caught market attention with a call to reopen debate on the unpopular use of tax money to deal with the huge bad loans weighing down the nation's financial institutions.
Some analysts applauded Kan for broaching what became a virtual political taboo after a huge outcry last year against using taxpayers' money to help wind up failed mortgage firms.
But others warned that Kan may have opened a political can of worms at a time when solutions to the problem are in short supply and voter antipathy to a public bailout remains strong.

"At least politicians have realised that bad loans are not shrinking and they can't solve the problem unless they use public funds," said Yushiro Ikuyo, first vice president at Smith Barney International. "But investors and analysts had high hopes last year...and then politicians and bureaucrats postponed any real solution, so there was huge disappointment."

Kan, a co-leader of the opposition Democratic Party who drew accolades last year when as health minister he exposed an AIDS scandal over tainted blood products, told television viewers on Sunday that parliament should debate both the proper disclosure of bad loans and the use public money to cope with the problem.

Ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) Secretary General Koichi Kato and his main opposition Shinshinto counterpart Takeo Nishioka agreed, although none of the three politicians went into details on how such funds might be used.

Some economists wondered whether Kan had thought deeply enough before broaching the touchy topic. "I think his comment is correct, but there is no idea about in what form public money should be used or in what sort of framework," said a Japanese economist who has advised Kan in the past.

Dismay over the failure of Japanese banks and other financial firms to make progress in writing off the bad loans left by the collapse of Japanese asset prices early this decade has dragged down Tokyo share prices since late last year.
Just how big the problem is, no one really knows -- hence the loud calls by analysts and investors for better disclosure.

The Finance Ministry estimates problem loans at commercial banks at about 35 trillion yen ($294 billion). But some private analysts say the banking sector is laden with some 100 trillion yen ($840 billion) in bad debt or potential bad debt, of which perhaps one-10th is not covered by assets and future profits.

"When faced with the question of just how much would be required to write off Japan's bankrupt financial institutions, the frank response...would probably be more than 10 trillion yen ($84 billion)," said a recent report by UBS Securities analyst Yukiko Ohara.

Of that, the Deposit Insurance Corp (DIC) -- a body which collects premiums from banks to protect depositors in the event of banking failures -- could likely cover three trillion yen ($25.2 billion) over five years, the report added.

"As it would still be difficult to raise the remainder even if deposit insurance rates were increased and the big banks were petitioned, the only route open is to inject public funds," the report said.

Such public money would be needed to help the government keep its pledge to protect depositors' money for the five years up to 2001, the same period during which Japan plans a sweeping "Big Bang" financial market deregulation that is expected to batter some of the weakest institutions even more.
Whether and how much tax money would have to be used will depend on how well government finance mandarins can manage the timing of financial institutions' failures, analysts said.

"Does the DIC have enough money to cover potential losses? The answer is that it depends on how successful the finance ministry is in controlling the flow of failures," said one foreign financial analyst. "If two regional banks go under (in a year)...maybe we could all sleep tight. But who's to say you won't have a situation in which 15 banks go under in one year."

A Finance Ministry official told Reuters on Monday that the ministry was not now considering any plan to use public money to deal with bad loan problems, and government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama rejected any such a move later in the day.

Reopening debate on the use of tax money to help solve the bad loan puzzle, however, risks rekindling the public outrage which flared last year over budgeting 685 billion yen ($5.75 billion) to help wind up failed "jusen" mortgage firms.
Much of the criticism focused on the government's failure to clarify who was to blame for the mess.
But full disclosure now of the banking system's bad loan woes without a workable plan to solve the problem could have devastating results, analysts warned.
Few, however, believe that either financial bureaucrats or politicians have any sweeping solutions up their sleeves.
"All the schemes until now have been a failure," the Japanese economist said. "No one, whether bureaucrat or politician, really knows what to do."
